1.pericope_label: Therefore, my brethren dearly beloved and longed for, my joy and crown, so stand fast in the Lord, my dearly beloved. I beseech Euodias, and beseech Syntyche, that they be of the same mind in the Lord. And I intreat thee also, true yokefellow, help those women which laboured with me in the gospel, with Clement also, and with other my fellowlabourers, whose names are in the book of life.

schools.summary: Read the opening word as a hinge, where a vision of future glory becomes the inspiring force behind sober present duties; note that longed for is a late and rare verbal adjective found here alone, and that the exhortation meets men tempted to defection, standing firm being hard once a panic starts; then handle the two women and the yokefellow as questions of evidence — the names attested in the inscriptions, the masculine vocative that sinks the proposal of Lydia, and the frank conclusion that it matters little who the peacemaker was.

Attend to the endearments and insist on what they are not, since Paul gains their hearts by lovely and kind names dictated by sincere affection rather than flattery, delighted to see men gained through his own instrumentality persevering; then resist the settled assumption of a quarrel, since the words afford no sufficient ground for the conjecture and he honours the two women enough to call them his fellow-soldiers in the gospel; and dispose of the reading that makes the yokefellow Paul's wife, the inference from the mention of women being excessively weak when Clement's name follows in the same breath.

Take the exhortation as continuity rather than novelty — so stand, as ye have done hitherto — and hear the doubled entreaty as the apostle speaking to each woman face to face with the utmost tenderness; then venture the reading that Euodias was a woman and Syntyche a man, probably her husband and the very yokefellow addressed next; or else name Silas, since Paul had many fellow-labourers but few yokefellows and Silas had been his yokefellow in that very city; and explain why women were needed for the work at all, where custom kept them from the apostles' reach.

Draw the inference from the close of the previous chapter, that since our conversation is in heaven and we look for the Saviour to come from there, the believing hope of eternal life should make us steady, even and constant in our Christian course; and note that the compellations are endearing because he means to carry his exhortation with the greater advantage.

debates.question: Were Euodias and Syntyche both women?

sides.position: Both women, doubtless, since the next verse refers to them; commonly supposed deaconesses, though there is no certain evidence of that
Euodias a woman and Syntyche a man, probably her husband, and the very yokefellow addressed in the next verse
Both women, and women of note at a city where the gospel was first preached to women and the church first met in a woman's house

debates.question: Was there a quarrel between them at all?

sides.position: It is the almost universally received opinion, but the words afford no sufficient ground for the conjecture, and Paul honours them enough to call them fellow-soldiers in the gospel
There was a disagreement, though whether about doctrine or something else cannot be determined from the phrase
In so pure a church even slight bickerings would make a real disturbance, and it may have been accidental friction between two energetic Christian women
Paul's own wife — an opinion as old as Clement of Alexandria, but untenable against what Paul says elsewhere of his unmarried state
holders: Clement of Alexandria (as reported by Ellicott)

sides.position: Not his wife: the word is masculine, and some take it for the proper name Syzygus
Lydia, which founders on the masculine vocative
Epaphroditus, a curious turn since he carried the letter
Silas, since Paul had many fellow-labourers but few yokefellows and Silas had been his yokefellow in that very city
It matters little that we do not know who the peacemaker was

outliers.note: Alone doubts that there was any quarrel to settle, holding that the text affords no sufficient ground for the conjecture and that the honour Paul pays the two women tells against it.

Alone collects the modern conjectures about the two women — that each had a congregation in her house, one Jewish and one Gentile; that they were ladies of rank; that in so pure a church even slight bickerings would make a real disturbance.

4.pericope_label: Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice. Let your moderation be known unto all men. The Lord is at hand. Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.

schools.summary: Recover the classical force of the greeting-word for joy while denying it is a greeting here, since the weight laid on it and the letter's constant returns to joy show the strict sense intended; render the disputed second term against strict duty, as the sense of what is seemly or equitable rather than what formal law requires — sweet reasonableness, the thing the world gropes after in good taste or right feeling; hear the command against anxiety as an exact repetition of the Lord's own take no thought; and take the closing verb as garrisoning, peace mounting guard like a sentinel.

Fit the command to rejoice to the moment, since with dangers on every side the Philippians might have given way, overcome by grief or impatience; weigh two readings of the second term and prefer enduring all things with equanimity, not easily moved by injuries nor easily annoyed by adversity; and insist that the closing sentence is a promise and not, as some make it by turning the future into an optative, a prayer — the peace of God guarding the whole soul so as to prevent a turning back from God in wicked thoughts or desires.

Read the repetition as showing not merely the apostle's earnestness but that the thing is God's will and their duty as well as their interest; gather the disputed word's whole range and borrow Macknight's definition entire — meekness under provocation, readiness to forgive injuries, equity in business, candour in judging others, sweetness of disposition, the entire government of the passions; press its reach to all men, since the roughest tempers are good-natured to some from natural sympathy while a Christian must be so to all; and set carefulness and prayer against each other as things that cannot stand together.

Begin from a contradiction and resolve it: Christ blessed those that mourn and pronounced woe on those that laugh, yet Paul commands rejoicing always — but the woe falls on the laughter of this world which arises from things present, and the blessing on those pricked at heart who mourn their own faults, so that this joy is not contrary to that grief but born out of it, the man who grieves for his sins and confesses them being the very man who rejoices.

debates.question: What does the disputed word rendered moderation mean?

sides.position: Restraint on the passions and general soberness of living, the root sense being what is fit or suitable
A very extensive range at once: mildness, patience, yieldingness, clemency, unwillingness to litigate, and the entire government of the passions
The sense of what is seemly or equitable as distinct from what strict duty requires, which the world gropes after in good taste or the spirit of a gentleman
Sweet reasonableness
Equanimity under injury and adversity rather than the giving up of one's right

debates.question: Is the closing sentence about peace a promise or a prayer?

sides.position: A promise, pointing out the advantage of firm confidence in God; the reading that turns the future into an optative is without proper foundation
A statement of what the peace of God does, garrisoning the heart as a sentinel mounts guard

outliers.note: Alone sets the command to rejoice against the beatitude on those that mourn and the woe on those that laugh, and resolves the two by making this joy the offspring of that grief.
Alone heads off the Stoic comparison the contentment word invites, insisting that Paul was no Stoic but had strong passions, all of them devoted to God.

8.pericope_label: Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things. Those things, which ye have both learned, and received, and heard, and seen in me, do: and the God of peace shall be with you.

schools.summary: Refuse to make a philosophic source of the list, since the adjectives are old-fashioned and familiar words rather than borrowings from any Stoic catalogue, and note that two of the six occur nowhere else in the New Testament; pair the terms so that truth is the inherent likeness to God and is thereby venerable, while just is righteousness in act and word as tested against a declared will and pure is righteousness in essence, in the thought that cannot be so tested; then take the appeal to example as a rule for the office, the preacher being the interpreter of the spiritual life and bound to be an instance of it.

Give the first term as nothing else than the integrity of a good conscience with its fruits, and then add what Paul does not reckon the rest sufficient without, that we endeavour to make ourselves agreeable to all so far as may lawfully be done in the Lord; and turn the appeal to his own life into a maxim about preaching, that the main thing in a public speaker is to speak not with his mouth merely but by his life, procuring authority for his doctrine by rectitude of living.

Refuse to let righteousness be sectional, so that they attend not to one branch of virtue but to everything bringing honour to God, good to their fellow creatures and credit to themselves; gloss the second term as grave, decent and venerable, whatever becomes a man as man, as citizen and as Christian; find the structure of the list in two rows of four, the first naming the duty and the second its commendation, word answering to word; and separate the four verbs of the last verse into their sources, what was learned, received by faith, heard publicly and privately, and seen at close quarters.

debates.question: Where does the list of excellences come from?

sides.position: Old-fashioned and familiar words, not necessarily drawn from any philosophic catalogue of moral excellencies, Stoic or otherwise
Things admitted to be true and good in the world which were never directly revealed, and which the Christian is nevertheless to exhibit
Whatever is really true even among the very heathens, as against falsehood and lying and hypocrisy

outliers.note: Alone applies the list to the present, judging the six ideals the more pertinent now that so much filth is flaunted before the world in books and magazines and moving-pictures under the name of realism.
Alone finds a structure in the list, eight particulars in two rows of four, the first row naming the duty and the second its commendation, with word answering to word.

10.pericope_label: But I rejoiced in the Lord greatly, that now at the last your care of me hath flourished again; wherein ye were also careful, but ye lacked opportunity. Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me. Notwithstanding ye have well done, that ye did communicate with my affliction.

schools.summary: Trace the verb for their revived care to Homer, to sprout or blossom again, and note it is transitive here, so that they caused their thinking of him to bloom afresh; hear in now at last a hitherto disappointed expectation, since Rome was the metropolis of universal concourse where earlier word might have been looked for; identify the contentment word as the Stoics' term for their ideal wise man, occurring nowhere else in the New Testament; and explain the verb for being instructed as the word for initiation into secret rites, so that the metaphor is drawn from the pagan mysteries.

Locate contentment in the disposition rather than the circumstances, since no man can be poor in mind who is satisfied with the lot assigned him by God, saints not measuring sufficiency by abundance; refuse the unlimited reading of the boast that follows, restraining it to the matter in hand since the apostle was not omnipotent and could not do all that Christ could; and mark how carefully Paul looks in both directions at once, guarding against the suspicion that want had broken him and equally against the appearance of despising their gift, which would be not merely obstinacy but haughtiness.

Keep the seasonal figure, that their care blossomed as a tree does after the winter, and make the delicate excuse for the interval, that they were careful but lacked opportunity or rather ability; head off the Stoic comparison in a line, that Paul was no Stoic but had strong passions, all of them devoted to God; notice the ascent of the four expressions, I have learned, I know, I am instructed, I can; and observe that the name of Christ is absent from the best manuscripts in the last of them.

Turn the thanks into a doctrine of giving, that almsgiving was introduced not for the sake of the receivers but of the givers, since the givers make the greatest gain; and read the apostle's praise as calculated in two directions at once, to keep those who had helped him from being lifted up with arrogance and to make them more zealous in well-doing, since the benefit returns upon themselves.

Credit the apostle with a grateful spirit, since he speaks of their kindness as though it were a piece of generous charity when it fell far short of a just debt, and what his friends did was nothing in comparison of what he deserved from them.

debates.question: Why had the Philippians been so long in sending?

sides.position: Not neglect or inattention, but the difficulty of communicating with him
They were careful but lacked opportunity, or rather lacked the ability
Either they had not plenty themselves, or they wanted a proper messenger
There is a note of hitherto disappointed expectation under the gladness, since at Rome earlier word might have been looked for than at Caesarea

debates.question: How far does I can do all things reach?

sides.position: Not without limitation, since the apostle was not omnipotent and could not do all that Christ could; it must be restrained to the matter in hand
Properly, I have strength in all things, and in this context to bear rather than to do, though the wider extension is not inadmissible
He could bear any trial and perform any duty, and this was neither vain self-reliance nor the mere result of experience
Not a habit acquired by frequent exercise but a disposition held by grace

outliers.note: Alone makes the passage a doctrine of almsgiving, that it was introduced for the sake of the givers rather than the receivers, since the givers make the greatest gain.
Alone observes that prosperity needs as much grace as adversity and perhaps more, since adversity of itself does something to keep the mind in a right state and prosperity does nothing.

15.pericope_label: Now ye Philippians know also, that in the beginning of the gospel, when I departed from Macedonia, no church communicated with me as concerning giving and receiving, but ye only. For even in Thessalonica ye sent once and again unto my necessity. Not because I desire a gift: but I desire fruit that may abound to your account. But I have all, and abound: I am full, having received of Epaphroditus the things which were sent from you, an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, wellpleasing to God. But my God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus. Now unto God and our Father be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

schools.summary: Take the mercantile language as the point, an account opened in the matter of giving and receiving, credit and debit, which no other church opened with him — not even Antioch contributed, and only later did Thessalonica and Beroea join Philippi in supporting the work at Corinth; note that the naming of the church is emphatic, marking the dignity of their exclusive position; observe that at rich and luxurious cities Paul refused maintenance and lived by his hands, what came from Philippi supplementing rather than superseding his own resources; and keep the figure to the end, God having an abundant treasure in glory out of which to repay them.

Read the recollection as an excuse rather than a boast, since a man who often receives may be thought too eager to receive, so that in clearing himself Paul praises them and in praising them modestly excuses the others; turn the caution on the reader, that we take heed lest the pious, seeing us too much inclined to receive, should on good grounds reckon us insatiable; and prefer the reading that makes the closing sentence an assertion rather than a wish, God owning as done to himself whatever kindness is shown to his servants.

Close on the doxology and what it presumes, that it is a great condescension and favour in God to own the relation of Father to sinners and to allow us to say Our Father — a title peculiar to the gospel dispensation, and an encouragement under all our weaknesses and fears to look upon him as one nearly related and tenderly affected towards us.

Note that while planting the church at Thessalonica Paul was supported partly by his own hands and partly by what came from Philippi, and add the unflattering observation that the Thessalonians themselves contributed little to his maintenance; then take the sweet smell as alluding to the sacrifices of the law, so that in what was done to his servant God is well pleased, and read the promise that follows as an exchange, that those who gave in his distress will never be suffered to want without help being raised up for them.

debates.question: Is the closing sentence about supply an assertion or a wish?

sides.position: A wish or prayer, as the Vulgate, Syriac and Arabic read it
holders: the Vulgate, Syriac and Arabic (as reported by Gill)

sides.position: An assertion by way of promise: he could not repay them, but his God would

outliers.note: Alone draws an unflattering comparison from the arrangement, noting that the Thessalonians themselves contributed little to Paul’s maintenance while he laboured among them.
Alone presses the book-keeping metaphor to its conclusion, that no other church opened an account with Paul, not even Antioch, and that Thessalonica and Beroea joined Philippi only later.

21.pericope_label: Salute every saint in Christ Jesus. The brethren which are with me greet you. All the saints salute you, chiefly they that are of Cesar’s household. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.  It was written to the Philippians from Rome by Epaphroditus.

schools.summary: Explain what the household means and what it does not, since the phrase covers not the imperial family but people attached to the establishment, slaves and freedmen and even the highest functionaries, so that the gospel is seen working upward from the lower classes; bring the evidence of the sepulchral inscriptions, where names greeted in Romans prove identical with members of the imperial household, and suggest the praetorian guard as the channel; then settle the benediction on textual grounds, the true reading being with your spirit, and dismiss the appended subscription as carrying no authority whatever though probably correct.

Call it no common evidence of divine mercy that the gospel made its way into that sink of all crimes and iniquities, the more to be admired because holiness rarely reigns in the courts of sovereigns; and reject the guess that Seneca was among the converts, since he never gave the smallest evidence of being a Christian and belonged not to the household but to the senate; then note what the closing benediction was for, being written in the apostle's own hand as the mark by which a letter of his was known to be genuine.

Keep the wonder small and sharp, that if even some of Nero's slaves were converted it would be marvellous enough, and report from Josephus that Poppaea was a worshipper of the true God and so may have put no hindrance in the way of servants who wished to believe; name the likely company of brethren from the other letters of the imprisonment; and list the textual evidence at the close, the word our absent from many manuscripts and versions, and Spirit read for all by a long line of uncials and by the Coptic, Sahidic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Vulgate and Old Latin.

debates.question: Who were they of Caesar's household?

sides.position: Not members of the imperial family but people attached to the establishment, a term covering slaves, freedmen and the highest functionaries
Possibly slaves, and if even some of Nero's slaves were converted it would be marvellous enough
Converts traceable by name, since many greeted in Romans match sepulchral inscriptions of the imperial household
Not Seneca, who never gave the smallest evidence of being a Christian and was a senator rather than of the household

debates.question: What is the true text of the closing benediction?

sides.position: Be with your spirit, the familiar reading being the more ordinary form of salutation
Spirit for all is read by a long line of uncials and by the Coptic, Sahidic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Vulgate and Old Latin, and our is absent from many witnesses
The Vulgate, the Ethiopic and the Alexandrian copy read with your spirit

outliers.note: Alone sets the prisoner against the emperor, observing that the gospel works upward from the lower classes and that Nero would kill himself shortly after Paul was executed.
Alone reports from Josephus that Poppaea was a worshipper of the true God, and infers that she may have put no hindrance in the way of servants who wished to believe.
